summary: This document defines an RTCP Extended Report block that reports a post-repair loss count metric for RTP applications. It also introduces a repaired loss count metric in the same block.

plainLanguage.summary: When some media packets go missing and are then recovered, this memo defines a small report that says how many are still missing and how many were recovered. It lets the sender judge how well its repair methods are working.

questions: how to report repaired packet loss in rtp
how to measure rtp loss repair effectiveness
subtitle: A compact RTCP report that tells a sender how many lost packets were fixed and how many stayed lost.

tldr.problem: Standard RTCP reports count packets lost before any repair, so a sender cannot tell how well retransmission or forward error correction is working. The existing per-packet report from RFC 5725 costs more bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7509 defines an RTCP XR block, block type 33, that carries a post-repair loss count and a repaired loss count over an explicit range of sequence numbers.
tldr.outcome: The sender or a third party can work out how many packets are still lost, how many were repaired and so how effective the repair methods are.

today: RFC 7509 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2015. The unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It provides a lower-overhead companion to the post-repair RLE block of RFC 5725.

sections.title: Why Pre-Repair Counts Are Not Enough
sections.content:
RTCP Sender and Receiver Reports (RFC 3550) include the cumulative number of packets lost. This document calls that the pre-repair loss metric, because it is measured on the media stream before any loss-repair mechanism, such as retransmission (RFC 4588) or Forward Error Correction (RFC 5109), is applied.

Recovering a packet does not reduce the fraction lost or the cumulative loss reported by those messages, so a sending endpoint cannot infer how well its repair mechanism performs from them alone. RFC 5725 addressed this with a post-repair loss Run-Length Encoding (RLE) report block, but its packet-by-packet reporting has a higher overhead than other report blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: The standard RTCP sender and receiver reports carry the cumulative number of packets lost. This memo calls that the pre-repair loss metric. It is measured before any repair mechanism, such as retransmission or forward error correction, is applied. Recovering a packet does not reduce the fraction lost or the cumulative loss those reports carry. A sender cannot tell from them how well its repair method is working. RFC 5725 added a post-repair report, but it reports packet by packet and costs more bandwidth than other report blocks.

sections.title: The Two New Metrics
sections.content:
The new block reports a post-repair loss count: the total number of packets finally lost after one or more loss-repair methods have been applied. It also reports a repaired loss count: the total number of packets fully repaired. Together with the pre-repair count, the repaired count lets an RTP sender or a third-party entity evaluate the effectiveness of the repair methods and calculate the pre-repair loss count over the same range.

Both metrics MUST measure only primary source RTP packets, the original packets the sender transmitted for the first time. They work at packet level, not slice or picture level, so partly recovering a packet does not count as repairing it. The metrics are measured at the RTP receiver and are applicable to any RTP application, especially those that use loss-repair mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: One number says how many lost things stayed lost. The other says how many were found again. Only the first copy of each thing counts, and a half-fixed packet does not count as fixed.

sections.title: The Report Block Format
sections.content:
The block is identified by Block Type (BT) 33. Its fields are:

  • Reserved (8 bits): MUST be set to zero by senders and ignored by receivers.
  • Block length (16 bits): MUST be 4. A block with any other value MUST be discarded.
  • SSRC of Source (32 bits): as defined in RFC 3611.
  • begin_seq (16 bits): the first sequence number the block reports on.
  • end_seq (16 bits): the last sequence number the block reports on, plus one.
  • Post-repair loss count (16 bits): total packets finally lost in that range. It MUST NOT count lost packets for which repair might still be possible.
  • Repaired loss count (16 bits): total packets fully repaired in that range.
sections.plainLanguage: The report is a small form. It names the stream, gives the first and last packet numbers it covers, and fills in two boxes: still lost and recovered.

sections.title: Cumulative and Interval Reports
sections.content:
Ambiguity can arise when this metric is compared with a pre-repair loss metric, because some packets not repaired in the current RTCP interval may be repaired later. The block therefore uses begin_seq and end_seq to state the actual sequence number range it covers, and only packets that have no further chance of being repaired, or that have been repaired, are included.

In a cumulative report, begin_seq is set to the first packet of the session and stays fixed. Combined with the cumulative loss from an RTCP Receiver Report, the sender can compute: still-to-be-repaired lost packets = cumulative number of packets lost - cumulative post-repair loss count - cumulative repaired loss count.

In an interval report, begin_seq and end_seq are aligned with the highest sequence numbers of consecutive Receiver Reports. This is NOT RECOMMENDED: in the RFC's example, packets 17 and 19 are lost in interval A and repaired in interval B, but interval B begins at 20, so they are never reported. Implementations that want them reported MUST NOT align the range to RTCP intervals. They may instead pick a range covering several intervals and overlapping earlier reports.
sections.plainLanguage:
Some packets not repaired in one RTCP interval may be repaired later. The block therefore states the exact range of sequence numbers it covers, using begin_seq and end_seq. Only packets that can no longer be repaired, or that have been repaired, are counted.

In a cumulative report, begin_seq stays at the first packet of the session. The sender can then subtract the post-repair and repaired counts from the cumulative loss. The result is the number of packets still waiting to be repaired. Aligning the range to each RTCP interval is NOT RECOMMENDED. A packet lost in one interval and repaired in the next would then never be reported. A report may instead cover several intervals and overlap earlier ones.

sections.title: Signaling with SDP
sections.content: RFC 3611 lets endpoints announce XR blocks in SDP (Session Description Protocol) with the rtcp-xr attribute, although XR blocks MAY also be used without prior signaling. This document augments that attribute with a new xr-format value, post-repair-loss-count, given by the ABNF xr-prlr-block = "post-repair-loss-count". In an offer/answer context, the rules for unilateral rtcp-xr parameters in RFC 3611 apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a call, each side can say it is able to send this kind of report by using a short agreed word.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The block introduces no new security considerations beyond RFC 3611, and because it does not provide per-packet statistics, the confidentiality risk documented there does not apply. An attacker could still put incorrect information in these reports, which would affect the performance of loss-repair mechanisms. Where security is a concern, implementations should apply encryption and authentication following the guidance in RFC 7202, for example using the AVPF profile together with Secure RTP (SAVPF, RFC 5124), though other mechanisms also exist.

IANA assigned block type value 33 in the RTCP XR Block Type Registry to the "Post-Repair Loss Count Metrics Report Block" and registered the SDP parameter post-repair-loss-count in the RTCP XR SDP Parameters Registry.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky person could write false numbers on the form, so important reports should be locked and signed.
